title: Harry Kane, James Milner and… Cristiano Ronaldo? Investigating accusations of stat-padding
content:
Two stalwarts of English football recently reached significant milestones in their careers.

Harry Kane scored his 500th goal for club and country when he netted for Bayern Munich against Werder Bremen, while Brighton & Hove Albion’s James Milner became the highest appearance maker in Premier League history, breaking Gareth Barry’s record.

However, the achievements — while both absolutely factually correct — came with caveats that led to heinous accusations of stat padding, ie, misleading factors bolstered their numbers.

In Kane’s case, of his first 500 goals (he has since progressed to 504), precisely 100 of those were scored from the penalty spot. Nothing wrong with that, obviously, but with penalties generally being quite easy to score, a point occasionally made about Kane’s goalscoring numbers is that they are inflated more than your average goalscorer by the number of penalties he scores.

Milner overtook Barry’s record of 653 appearances when starting for Brighton against Brentford last month, but look a little deeper and you realise Barry had actually played around 14,000 minutes more than Milner, owing to Milner making far more substitute appearances.

Is that another form of unintentional stat padding? Do Kane and Milner’s records mean any less, given that extra context? And what are other examples of stat padding in football? Let’s investigate.

Taking penalties is certainly a good idea if you want to break records and sit in a lofty position in all-time goalscorer charts.

Kane is second in the list of Premier League top scorers behind Alan Shearer, with 213 goals. Of those, 33 were penalties, accounting for 15.5 per cent of his goals. If Kane weren’t a penalty taker, like, say, Andrew Cole or Les Ferdinand, he would be seventh, nestled behind Cole and between Sergio Aguero (sixth) and Frank Lampard (eighth) on 180 goals.

Cole very rarely took penalties, netting only one among his Premier League total of 187 goals. Playing for Manchester United and Newcastle United in the 1990s and early 2000s, you can imagine Cole could easily have added 2o to 30 goals to his overall tally and put himself behind only Shearer in the all-time list had he been either club’s main penalty taker.

Ferdinand, who played predominantly for Tottenham Hotspur, Newcastle and Queens Park Rangers, is the highest-scoring Premier League player to have never scored (or even taken) a penalty, with all 149 of his goals coming from other sources.

Why didn't Ferdinand take penalties? The Athletic asked him some years ago, and the reply was blunt: "Stupidity. When I think about it now… when I got into the team (at QPR), there was already a penalty-taker. Roy Wegerle took them, then Clive Wilson started taking them. He had an exemplary record and then when I went to Newcastle, Peter Beardsley would take them (before Shearer).

"But the truth is, if I’d have said, ‘I want to take them’, I don’t think anyone would have stopped me. But then I had that (thought), ‘I’m going to go through my career without taking a penalty and see how many goals I’m going to score’. That’s what I thought back then. But do you know what? I regret it."

Of the Premier League's top 35 goalscorers, Sadio Mane (111 goals) and Emile Heskey (110) are the only other players who did not add to their tally with a penalty, while Cole, Paul Scholes (107 goals) and Peter Crouch (108) only scored one.

Didier Drogba (four penalties in 104 goals), Dwight Yorke (six in 123), Nicolas Anelka (seven in 125) and Romelu Lukaku (seven in 121) are the other strikers on the top scorer list who scored fewer than 10 Premier League penalties.

While Ferdinand went down the bullish route of trying to score as many goals as he could without needing the easier route of penalties, Shearer was the opposite, scoring 56 in his record tally of 260 goals.

In terms of the percentage of his goals that were penalties, Shearer is the greediest striker on the top-scorers' list, with 21.5 per cent of his goals coming via that route, but three players can beat his xG (in this case, expected greediness) rating; Frank Lampard on 24.3 per cent (43 penalties of 177 goals), Matt Le Tissier on 25 per cent (25 penalties of 100 goals) and Steven Gerrard, whose 32 penalties in a tally of 120 Premier League goals accounted for 26.7 per cent of all his goals.

Kane's aforementioned 15.5 per cent places him ninth in that percentage ranking.

No statistical deep dive into the percentage of penalties of a goalscorer's overall tally would be complete without comparing Lionel Messi and Ferdinand. No, just joking, we mean Messi and that chap Cristiano Ronaldo, who famously enjoy being compared to one another.

Messi has scored 898 career goals for Barcelona, Paris Saint-Germain, Inter Miami and Argentina. Of those 898, 112 have been penalties, or 12.4 per cent.

Ronaldo, for Sporting CP, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus, Al Nassr and Portugal, has scored more goals and more penalties, with 965 goals and 182 spot kicks, or 18.8 per cent.

A penalty is pretty easy in goalscoring terms, but it's still harder than a five-yard tap-in, at least according to xG, so in the Premier League, who are the stat-padders boosting their numbers by only scoring easy chances?

The boffins at Opta provided us with data going back to 2018-19, specifically on players who have scored the most non-penalty goals with the highest percentage of their chances being at a rating of 0.3xG or above — ie, which players are consistently scoring most of their goals via chances which are judged to be fairly straightforward?

The 0.3xG figure represents a pretty decent opportunity. Trent Alexander-Arnold, for example, has never scored a Premier League goal that has an xG rating of 0.3 or above. (The guy only scores free kicks and worldies.)

If you were going to guess which renowned Premier League tap-in merchant would top this list, somebody who mostly hung around in opposition penalty boxes like a fox, or just incessantly made runs beyond the last man, like a fox who had downed three energy drinks before kick-off, who would you pick? That's right, Ismaila Sarr.

It turns out Crystal Palace's wide forward just loves ghosting in at the back stick for a tap-in, with 68 per cent of his Premier League goals coming via chances from an xG rating of 0.3 or above.

Sarr is joint-leader in that list, with the guy you may have been thinking of a second ago, Jamie Vardy, who scored far more non-penalty goals than Sarr in that time period (66 to 22), but also registered 68 per cent of those goals from good scoring opportunities.

Also high on the list: Callum Wilson (63 per cent), Kai Havertz (62 per cent), Raheem Sterling (61 per cent), Gabriel Jesus (60 per cent), Mane (60 per cent), Tammy Abraham (59 per cent), Eddie Nketiah (58 per cent) and Dominic Calvert-Lewin (58 per cent).

When looking at this season only, Jean-Philippe Mateta (80 per cent) tops the tap-in standings, ahead of Calvert-Lewin (75 per cent) and Kevin Schade (71 per cent), while Viktor Gyokeres, a striker perhaps deliberately signed to be a stat-padding, flat-track bully, is seventh on 62 per cent.

When we say a footballer has made X number of appearances in a season, that only tells you how many times they have stepped onto the pitch, but clearly, that's not the whole story.

For example, Gabriel Jesus has scored five goals in 18 appearances in all competitions in 2025-26, not a fantastic tally for a striker, but it would be unfair to the Brazilian not to point out he has made only six starts in those 18 games. In fact, his five goals come from 675 minutes of football, working out as a goal every 135 minutes, a much nicer statistic for Jesus to put on his CV.

Likewise, a player who has had 38 starts will likely have made much more of a contribution than a player who makes 38 substitute appearances.

Which brings us back to Milner and his conflated data, with a high percentage of his appearances, at least in recent years, coming off the bench. Milner hasn't started 20 Premier League matches in a single season since 2016-17, when he started 36 times for Liverpool. His highest number of starts in the nine seasons since is 19 (in 2018-19).

Of the top 10 appearance-makers in Premier League history, a list which Milner now sits at No 1, the 40-year-old utility man has made the lowest percentage of starts by some distance.

Of his 654 appearances, 67 per cent of them (436 appearances) have been as a starter. The next lowest starter is 83 per cent for Ryan Giggs, who made 522 starts in his 632 Premier League appearances for Manchester United.

Sol Campbell (503 appearances) and the late Gary Speed (535 appearances) both register the highest percentage of starts in their games played, with 97 per cent, while Barry is not far behind on 95 per cent.

Of other players who have played a lot of Premier League football, Milner's 67 per cent of starts is similar to Crouch, who started 66 per cent of his games. Crouch was often a substitute during the later years of his career at Stoke City, but also for long periods at Spurs and Liverpool.

Unsurprisingly, Crouch's one-time strike partner at Spurs and Portsmouth, Jermain Defoe, is also high on the super-sub appearance list, with 70 per cent of his 496 Premier League games coming as starts.

Moving lower down the all-time Premier League appearance list, some players featured hundreds of times in the division, with only around half of them coming as starts.

Shane Long played 344 times, but only 54 per cent of those were from the beginning of a game, while Brighton's Danny Welbeck isn't much higher (62 per cent of starts from his 389 top-flight matches).

Among active players, Adama Traore, now of West Ham United, is well versed in beginning matches on the bench, with only 46 per cent of his 265 Premier League appearances coming in a starting XI.

Former Arsenal striker Nketiah, now at Crystal Palace, can top that with just 31 per cent of starts in 157 games, the same percentage as notoriously effective substitute Divock Origi (127 Premier League appearances, 40 starts).

Zoom down the list and the percentage goes all the way to zero, with many players able to say they have played in the Premier League, but never as a starter.

They include 21-year-old Spurs striker Dane Scarlett (now on loan with Hibernian in Scotland), who has played 11 times off the bench in the Premier League but never been named in a starting XI.

All of Wales international midfielder Jonny Williams' 12 Premier League appearances for Crystal Palace came off the bench, while current Palace bench-warmer Christantus Uche has just overtaken him on 13 appearances and no starts.

In fact, there's a theme here, because at the top of the sub-but-never-started list, with almost double the tally of the man in second place (ex-Leeds United midfielder Ian Poveda, with 14 sub appearances), is another Palace man, midfielder Naouirou Ahamada.

The France youth international moved to Selhurst Park from Stuttgart in 2023 and made a total of 28 Premier League appearances… all from the bench. Ahamada, then, is the ultimate Premier League appearance stat-padder, with almost a season's worth of matches under his belt, but no starts.

The 23-year-old left Palace in January and, thankfully, is now a regular starter for Auxerre in Ligue 1, having remembered to put his kit on before kick-off for the first time in a long while.
